stdout_tail:
Done. `analysis.py` and `result.json` are written.

## Finding

**Yes — model family affects performance, but how much depends entirely on which families you're comparing.**

Held-out test ROC-AUC (stratified 80/20, seed 42):

| Model | ROC-AUC | PR-AUC | Acc | F1(>50K) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HistGradientBoosting | **0.9258** | 0.820 | 0.870 | 0.706 |
| RandomForest | 0.9151 | 0.794 | 0.863 | 0.683 |
| LogisticRegression | 0.9029 | 0.758 | 0.849 | 0.652 |
| DecisionTree | 0.8952 | 0.768 | 0.854 | 0.668 |
| kNN (k=25) | 0.8923 | 0.721 | 0.840 | 0.644 |
| GaussianNB | 0.8275 | 0.528 | 0.622 | 0.540 |

**Primary metric: +0.0229 ROC-AUC (boosting − logistic regression)**, 95% paired-bootstrap CI [+0.0197, +0.0260] — real and unambiguous, but modest. The best-vs-worst spread across all six families is 0.098, i.e. ~4× larger. The honest reading: choosing *badly* (Gaussian NB, whose independence assumption is badly violated here) costs a lot; choosing among competent families costs little. Boosting > forest is itself significant (+0.0107 [+0.0085, +0.0129]).

## Stability check

It held up cleanly under both checks:
- **5×5 repeated stratified CV** (25 fits/family): boosting mean AUC 0.9293 (sd 0.0023) vs 0.9065 for logistic; per-fold paired gap +0.0228 (sd 0.0015, range 0.0201–0.0257), boosting won **25/25 folds**. Top-3 ordering identical in 25/25 folds; full 6-way ordering in 24/25 (only the near-tied DecisionTree/kNN pair swaps).
- **Fresh seed-2024 hold-out** never touched by the primary analysis: gap +0.0229 — essentially identical.

## Caveats worth flagging

The biggest lever another researcher would pull differently: **I gave every family sensible defaults and spent no tuning budget**. That's a deliberately even-handed protocol, but it isn't neutral — boosting's defaults are near-optimal on tabular data, while logistic regression's are not (no splines, no interactions), so the ~0.023 gap is best read as an upper bound on the family effect. I also dropped `fnlwgt` (a census sampling weight, not a person-level attribute) and 52 duplicate rows, and encoded missing categoricals as an explicit `Missing` level rather than imputing them.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the size of the effect depends on which families you compare. Gradient boosting is the clear winner: on a held-out 20% test set HistGradientBoosting reached ROC-AUC 0.9258 versus 0.9029 for logistic regression, a gap of +0.0229 (95% paired-bootstrap CI [+0.0197, +0.0260]) -- statistically unambiguous but modest in practice. Across all six families the spread is much larger (0.098 AUC, HistGradientBoosting 0.926 down to GaussianNB 0.828), so model family choice matters a great deal at the low end and only marginally among the strong learners (boosting, random forest, logistic regression all >= 0.90).
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (HistGradientBoosting - LogisticRegression), held-out test set
parsed_result.direction: HistGradientBoosting > RandomForest > LogisticRegression > DecisionTree ~ kNN >> GaussianNB; model family does affect performance, but the boosting-vs-logistic gap is small (~0.023 ROC-AUC) while the best-vs-worst spread is ~0.10
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Six model families on one common feature space: LogisticRegression (L2, C=1, max_iter=2000), GaussianNB, kNN (k=25), DecisionTree (min_samples_leaf=20), RandomForest (400 trees, min_samples_leaf=2), HistGradientBoosting (300 iters, lr=0.1). Preprocessing: dropped 52 exact duplicate rows and the fnlwgt column (a census sampling weight, not a person-level attribute); missing categoricals (workclass/occupation/native-country) encoded as an explicit 'Missing' level rather than imputed; one-hot encoding with min_frequency=10 and handle_unknown='ignore'; median imputation + standardisation of numerics for the scale-sensitive models (linear/kNN/NB), unscaled for trees. Kept both 'education' and 'education-num' despite redundancy. Primary metric ROC-AUC (threshold-free, robust to the 24% positive rate); PR-AUC, accuracy and positive-class F1 at threshold 0.5 reported alongside. No class-imbalance reweighting or resampling, and deliberately NO per-model hyperparameter tuning -- every family got sensible library defaults, which is the main lever another researcher could pull differently (a tuned kNN/SVM or a tuned logistic regression with splines/interactions would narrow the gap). Validation: single stratified 80/20 hold-out (seed 42) with a 2000-resample paired bootstrap over test rows for the pairwise AUC differences.
parsed_result.verification_method: Two independent checks. (A) 5x5-fold repeated stratified cross-validation (25 fits per family, RepeatedStratifiedKFold seed 7, a different model random seed per fold) over the full dataset, comparing mean AUC, per-fold paired gaps and mean rank stability. (B) A second, completely fresh stratified 80/20 hold-out split (seed 2024) not used anywhere in the primary analysis.
parsed_result.verification_result: Held up. (A) In 5x5 repeated CV HistGradientBoosting ranked first with mean AUC 0.9293 (sd 0.0023) vs 0.9065 for logistic regression; the paired per-fold gap was +0.0228 (sd 0.0015, range [+0.0201, +0.0257]) and boosting beat logistic regression in 25/25 folds. The full best-to-worst family spread was 0.101 AUC; the top-3 ordering (boosting > forest > logistic) was identical in 25/25 folds and the full 6-way ordering in 24/25 (only the near-tied DecisionTree/kNN pair ever swaps). (B) On the fresh seed-2024 hold-out the winner was HistGradientBoosting with a gap of +0.0229 over logistic regression and a spread of 0.083. Revised estimate for the boosting-vs-logistic gap: ~0.023 ROC-AUC (plausible range 0.020-0.026).
